items.readable_text:
Content:
Let [MATH: \triangle{ABC}] be a triangle where the lengths [MATH: AB=7] and [MATH: AC=5] are fixed. For example, consider the triangle shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/891c8afde059adfc6e3a52212a4cd32b]

Content:
Now, suppose that we vary the angle [MATH: \angle{A}], making it either very small or very large. What would be the maximum possible length of the side [MATH: \overline {BC}] for which the figure is still a triangle?

Content:
We make the longest possible segment [MATH: \overline{BC}] by increasing the angle [MATH: \angle{A}] as shown in the sketches below. Here, we fix vertices [MATH: A] and [MATH: B], and then "rotate" the side [MATH: \overline{AC}] about the vertex [MATH: A] until [MATH: \angle{A}] measures [MATH: 180^\circ.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3f355279d6514e3add9a6d8f1fb64157]

Content:
From the picture, we can see that when [MATH: m\angle{A}=180^\circ ,] we will not have a triangle anymore and the length of [MATH: \overline{BC}] will be [MATH: 7+5=12.] Therefore, if we would like to have a triangle, [MATH: \overline{BC}] must be shorter than the sum of the other sides:
[MATH: BC|< AB + AC; < 7 + 5; < 12]

Content:
This is true for all triangles:

Content:
> In every triangle, the length of any one side must be smaller than the sum of the other two sides.

Content:
The above statement is one part of the triangle inequality theorem, which we will continue building upon in this lesson.

items.title: Identifying Impossible Sides of a Triangle

sections.normalized_html: Is it possible that the lengths of the sides of a triangle are [MATH: 10, 15,] and [MATH: 25?]
sections.readable_text: Is it possible that the lengths of the sides of a triangle are [MATH: 10, 15,] and [MATH: 25?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The triangle inequality theorem states that the length of any one side must be smaller than the sum of the other two sides.

In particular, for the numbers [MATH: 10,15,25] to represent the sides of a triangle, the number [MATH: 25] must be smaller than the sum of the numbers [MATH: 10] and [MATH: 15.] But this is not the case: [MATH: 10 + 15 = 25 \not> 25] Therefore, the three numbers [MATH: 10,15,25] cannot represent the sides of a triangle.

items.title: The Triangle Inequality Theorem

sections.normalized_html: All of the discussion so far can be summarized in the following statement that is called the triangle inequality theorem.
sections.readable_text: All of the discussion so far can be summarized in the following statement that is called the triangle inequality theorem.

sections.normalized_html: In a triangle, the length of a side must be greater than the difference of the lengths of the other two sides and less than the sum of those lengths.
sections.readable_text: > In a triangle, the length of a side must be greater than the difference of the lengths of the other two sides and less than the sum of those lengths.

sections.normalized_html: Let's write that down using mathematical notations. Suppose that in a triangle the length of a side equals [MATH: a] and the other two sides have length [MATH: b] and [MATH: c] with [MATH: b>c.] Then, we must have [MATH: b - c < a < b + c.]

[MATH: b - c < a < b + c.]

Content:
All of the discussion so far can be summarized in the following statement that is called the triangle inequality theorem.

Content:
> In a triangle, the length of a side must be greater than the difference of the lengths of the other two sides and less than the sum of those lengths.

Content:
Let's write that down using mathematical notations. Suppose that in a triangle the length of a side equals [MATH: a] and the other two sides have length [MATH: b] and [MATH: c] with [MATH: b>c.] Then, we must have
[MATH: b - c < a < b + c.]

Content:
If we would like to omit the assumption that [MATH: b>c], we can still use the same inequality, as long as we include an absolute value on the left-hand side:
[MATH: | b - c | < a < b + c]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The triangle inequality theorem states that the length of any one side must be smaller than the sum of the other two sides.

  • Applying the triangle inequality theorem to [MATH: \triangle{ADC}], we get [MATH: AC|< AD + DC; AC|< 26cm + 13cm; AC|< 39cm.]

  • Applying the triangle inequality theorem to [MATH: \triangle{ABC}], we get [MATH: AC|< AB + BC; AC|< 12cm + 10cm; AC|< 22cm.]

Since both [MATH: AC < 39\,\textrm{cm}] and [MATH: AC < 22\,\textrm{cm}] must be satisfied, we conclude that

[MATH: AC < 22\,\textrm{cm}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:

Content:
Now, suppose that we vary the angle [MATH: \angle{A}], making it either very small or very large. What would be the maximum possible length of the side [MATH: \overline {BC}] for which the figure is still a triangle?

Content:
We make the longest possible segment [MATH: \overline{BC}] by increasing the angle [MATH: \angle{A}] as shown in the sketches below. Here, we fix vertices [MATH: A] and [MATH: B], and then "rotate" the side [MATH: \overline{AC}] about the vertex [MATH: A] until [MATH: \angle{A}] measures [MATH: 180^\circ.]

Content:
From the picture, we can see that when [MATH: m\angle{A}=180^\circ ,] we will not have a triangle anymore and the length of [MATH: \overline{BC}] will be [MATH: 7+5=12.] Therefore, if we would like to have a triangle, [MATH: \overline{BC}] must be shorter than the sum of the other sides:
[MATH: BC|< AB + AC; < 7 + 5; < 12]

Content:
This is true for all triangles:

Content:
> In every triangle, the length of any one side must be smaller than the sum of the other two sides.

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Impossible Sides of a Triangle

Example Prompt:
Is it possible that the lengths of the sides of a triangle are [MATH: 10, 15,] and [MATH: 25?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The triangle inequality theorem states that the length of any one side must be smaller than the sum of the other two sides.

In particular, for the numbers [MATH: 10,15,25] to represent the sides of a triangle, the number [MATH: 25] must be smaller than the sum of the numbers [MATH: 10] and [MATH: 15.] But this is not the case:
[MATH: 10 + 15 = 25 \not> 25]
Therefore, the three numbers [MATH: 10,15,25] cannot represent the sides of a triangle.

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Difference of Two Sides

Consider the same triangle as before, with sides [MATH: 5] and [MATH: 7.] This time, what is the shortest possible length of the side [MATH: \overline {BC},] for which the figure is still a triangle?

We make the shortest possible segment [MATH: \overline{BC}] by decreasing the angle [MATH: \angle{A}.] Again, we fix [MATH: A] and [MATH: B], and then "rotate" the side [MATH: \overline{AC}] about the vertex [MATH: A] towards the side [MATH: \overline{AB}.]

Item 6 — Tutorial: The Triangle Inequality Theorem

Content:
All of the discussion so far can be summarized in the following statement that is called the triangle inequality theorem.

Content:
> In a triangle, the length of a side must be greater than the difference of the lengths of the other two sides and less than the sum of those lengths.

Content:
Let's write that down using mathematical notations. Suppose that in a triangle the length of a side equals [MATH: a] and the other two sides have length [MATH: b] and [MATH: c] with [MATH: b>c.] Then, we must have
[MATH: b - c < a < b + c.]

Content:
If we would like to omit the assumption that [MATH: b>c], we can still use the same inequality, as long as we include an absolute value on the left-hand side:
[MATH: | b - c | < a < b + c]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
According to the triangle inequality theorem, the length of any side must be

- greater than the difference between the lengths of the other two sides, and
- less than the sum of those lengths.

Therefore, we have
[MATH: Difference|< x < Sum; 7 − 1|< x < 7 + 1; 6|< x < 8.]

Item 10 — Example: Finding the Maximum or Minimum Length of a Side of a Triangle: Word Problems

Example Prompt:
Paul knows that the distance between cell tower [MATH: A] and cell tower [MATH: B] is [MATH: 35\,\textrm{miles},] and the distance between cell tower [MATH: B] and cell tower [MATH: C] is [MATH: 25\,\textrm{miles},] but he does not know their exact locations. Assuming that the three locations form a triangle, what is the range of possible values for the distance between cellphone towers [MATH: A] and [MATH: C?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we let:

- [MATH: A] be the position of the tower [MATH: A]
- [MATH: B] be the position of the tower [MATH: B]
- [MATH: C] be the position of the tower [MATH: C]

Let's draw [MATH: \triangle ABC.]

[IMG: /graphics/7edbc7025fff692adb48a0b52bbe5d97]

We know that
[MATH: AB = 35\,\textrm{mi}, \qquad BC = 25\,\textrm{mi}.]

According to the triangle inequality theorem,
[MATH: AB − BC|< AC < AB + BC; 35 − 25|< AC < 35 + 25; 10|< AC < 60.]

Therefore, the distance from the tower [MATH: A] to the tower [MATH: C] must be between [MATH: 10 \,\textrm{mi}] and [MATH: 60 \,\textrm{mi}].
